facts.title: Predicted Before It Was Found
facts.text: In 1871 Dmitri Mendeleev left a gap in his periodic table for a missing element he called "eka-aluminium," predicting its atomic weight, density, and even that it would have a low melting point. Just four years later, in 1875, the French chemist Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran isolated it and confirmed the predictions almost exactly. This stunning success helped convince skeptical scientists that the periodic table was a genuine law of nature, not a coincidence.

facts.title: A Patriotic (and Sneaky) Name
facts.text: Boisbaudran named the element gallium after Gallia, the Latin name for France, his homeland. Some chemists have long suspected a hidden pun, because "Lecoq" means "the rooster" in French, and the Latin word for rooster is gallus. Boisbaudran denied any wordplay, but the coincidence has delighted chemistry students for nearly 150 years.

facts.title: It Melts in Your Hand
facts.text: Gallium has a melting point of just 29.76 degrees Celsius (about 85.6 degrees Fahrenheit), low enough that a solid chunk turns to liquid in the warmth of your palm. Yet it does not boil until around 2,400 degrees Celsius, giving it one of the largest liquid temperature ranges of any element. This odd combination makes it useful in high-temperature thermometers where mercury would boil away.

facts.title: The Spoon That Vanishes
facts.text: Because gallium is solid at room temperature but melts near body temperature, chemists use it to make a classic prank: a spoon that dissolves into a hot cup of tea. Gallium is also far less toxic than mercury, the other famous room-temperature-adjacent metal, which is why it is sometimes called a safer liquid metal. Despite melting easily, it is not something to eat, but handling it briefly is generally harmless.

facts.title: It Expands When It Freezes
facts.text: Like water, ice, and only a handful of other substances such as bismuth and silicon, gallium is denser as a liquid than as a solid, so it expands when it solidifies. This means freezing gallium can crack its container, so it is never stored in completely full sealed glass or metal vessels. This anomaly comes from the unusual way its atoms pack together in the crystal.

facts.title: The Heart of Modern Electronics
facts.text: Gallium's most important use is in compound semiconductors, especially gallium arsenide (GaAs) and gallium nitride (GaN). GaN is what makes the blue and white LEDs in your phone screen and modern light bulbs possible, an achievement that won the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics. GaAs powers high-speed chips in satellites, radar, and 5G base stations because electrons move through it faster than through ordinary silicon.

facts.title: No Mining Required
facts.text: There is no such thing as a gallium mine, because the element is too scattered to form its own ore deposits. Instead, it is recovered as a byproduct of refining aluminium from bauxite and processing zinc ores. The average crust contains gallium at roughly 19 parts per million, similar to lead, but it is almost always thinly diluted inside other minerals.

facts.title: A Spy Inside Your Bones
facts.text: Doctors use radioactive gallium-67 and gallium-68 as tracers in medical imaging. Because gallium ions behave chemically a bit like iron, the body transports them to sites of infection, inflammation, and certain tumors, where scanners can detect the faint radiation. Gallium-68 PET scans are now a powerful tool for finding prostate cancer and neuroendocrine tumors with remarkable precision.

facts.title: Liquid Metal That Heals Itself
facts.text: Alloys of gallium with indium and tin, such as galinstan, stay liquid well below room temperature and conduct electricity, making them candidates for flexible, stretchable, and self-healing circuits. Researchers are exploring these liquid metals for soft robotics and wearable electronics that can bend without breaking. Gallium-based coolants are also studied for chips because liquid metal carries heat far better than water.

facts.title: It Quietly Attacks Aluminium
facts.text: A small amount of liquid gallium can soak into aluminium along its grain boundaries and make the strong metal crumble like a cracker, a process called liquid metal embrittlement. For this reason gallium is banned from aircraft cabins and carefully kept away from aluminium structures. The same property fascinates materials scientists studying how metals fail at the atomic scale.
